Extrapolation of the findings were undertaken by analysing Prediction of Clinical Outcomes from Genomic Profiles (PRECOG) and Cell type Identification By Estimating Relative Subsets Of known RNA Transcripts (CIBERSORT) datasets. Having previously identified cancer stem cells, we herein identified a near absence of NK cells in the BCC tumour immune infiltrate. NK cells were sufficient to kill BCC cells in co-culture. Yet in situ, CD200 undergoes ectodomain shedding by metalloproteinases (MMP-3 and MMP-11) releasing biologically active soluble CD200 into the BCC microenvironment. CD200 binds its cognate receptor on NK cells to block tumour cell killing. Moreover, inactivation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway simultaneously leads to peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)-c dependent transcription of the death receptor pathway members. NK cell membrane accumulation of the Fas/Fas-associated protein with death domain death receptor and its ligand, FasL, led to activation-induced apoptosis. Blocking CD200 signalling or PPAR-c was sufficient to prevent NK cell apoptosis. Analysis of 20 cancer types in the PRECOG dataset identified CD200-mediated NK cell depletion as a shared mechanism in many cancer types. CD200-mediated NK cell depletion appears to be associated with poor outcome for many cancers and thus represents a novel targetable NK cell-specific immune checkpoint. P60 Merkel cell cancer: the need to standardize care Beenish Afzal, Sulaiman Tomy, Caroline Bridgewater, Laura Keeling and Ruth Murphy Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, Sheffield, UK; and University of Sheffield Medical School, Sheffield, UK Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is a rare but a highly aggressive cutaneous neuroendocrine neoplasia. In 2010 the MCC incidence rate was estimated to be 0.1–0.2 per 100 000 in England, which equates to 53–106 people a year (https://www. nice.org.uk/guidance/ta517/documents/final-scope). Typically, MCC presents as a rapidly growing, nontender, red nodule on an elderly person; however, due to nonspecific and varied characteristics, it can present as a diagnostic challenge, potentially leading to a delay in diagnosis and commencement of treatment. Currently, there are no National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines for treating MCC. Localized disease tends to be treated surgically with or without radiotherapy or radiotherapy alone. Metastatic disease is treated with chemotherapy; however, in July 2021 NICE approved avelumab as a treatment option for metastatic MCC in patients who have not had any prior chemotherapy. We looked at the 5-year data of all patients with MCC discussed at regional specialized skin cancer multidisciplinary team meetings from 2016 to 2020. The aim was to understand the patient population, presentation of MCC, the current patient pathway, and to compare the investigations and recommended treatment options with European and American guidelines for MCC. Among the cohort of 59 patients, 58% (n = 34) were male and 42% (n = 25) were female. The most common age group at presentation was 80–89 years, with 54% of the cases falling in this age range. The head and neck (52%) were the most common anatomical areas involved. Most cases (69%) were 2week wait referrals for ‘a rapidly growing lesion’. None was referred as possible MCC and only 11 had MCC as part of their differential diagnoses after being reviewed in secondary care. The most common differentials were squamous cell carcinoma (23%) and basal cell carcinoma (15%). The majority (64%) of these patients received radiotherapy; others elected for surgery alone and some elected for no treatment. None of the patients were tested for Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV) oncoprotein antibodies. Recent American guidelines for MCC suggest that MCPyV oncoprotein antibody testing should be performed in initial workup and may help guide surveillance. Furthermore only 18% of the patients had sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) done, whereas American guidelines recommend SLNB in every clinically node-negative patient who is fit for surgery (https://merkelcell.org/wp-content/uploads/ 2021/02/NCCN-2021.pdf). MCC is an aggressive tumour that appears to be poorly recognized in both primary and secondary care. These data suggest the need for greater recognition of this tumour and the need for national guidelines to standardize patient care.

title: All is balanced: inter‐ α ‐trypsin inhibitors as unseen extracellular matrix proteins in epidermal morphology and differentiation
abstract: A growing number of epidermal diseases have been attributed to defects in epidermal structure, such as the cytoskeleton or cellular junctions, in terminal keratinocyte differentiation and the well-levelled linkage and detachment of corneocytes, and in signalling pathways for instance leading to altered proliferative properties of keratinocytes 1, 2. Many of these processes rely on the readiness of proteases. Given their vast importance in organ development and maintenance, their activity has to be controlled on different levels, not only must they be available in the right moment of cellular differentiation, but also have to be instantly switchable. A large number of different proteases are therefore synthesized in different layers of the skin, and they are closely controlled by a collection of protease inhibitors. The importance of protease cascades is illustrated by the fact that several skin diseases can be caused by mutations in a single protease or protease inhibitor 3, which would lead to disturbed cornification and eventually a defective epidermal barrier function. Recent developments in genetics and genomics have resulted in the identification of numerous mutations that cause monogenic skin diseases; however, our knowledge about the molecular pathogenesis of these diseases and especially multifactorial skin diseases is still rather limited. New generations of sequencing technologies have facilitated high-throughput approaches to study DNA sequences and gene expression with growing depth and speed. The understanding of global gene expression profiles, however, is still hindered by both technical and biological limitations. The analysis of the transcriptome has become possible, at least for single cell types and tissues, using microarray-based methods, and these approaches have already resulted in an accumulation of large amounts of valuable data. In contrast, the analysis of certain developmental (or pathological) processes and the comparison of large numbers of samples are quite arduous and thus restricted with these methods. The use of high-throughput sequencing for transcriptome analysis with RNA-seq has made these studies possible 4, 5. On the other hand, disadvantages of either method have been widely discussed; while the detection rates for various transcripts are much bigger with RNA-seq, limitations in the discovery of differential expression of poorly expressed genes have to be taken into account 6. Expression analyses of single genes or gene families using high-throughput approaches thus allow thorough studies of cell-type or disease-specific gene expression patterns and open new possibilities for the characterization of pathologies and mechanisms involved in the development of multifactorial disorders. One such gene family, which has been only poorly characterized so far and mostly in the context of tumor development, is the family of inter-α-trypsin inhibitors (ITIs), a group of plasma serine protease inhibitors. ITIs consist of a light chain, also referred to as bikunin (OMIM 176870), and a number of various heavy chains (ITIH1–ITIH6). ITI heavy chains are supposed to play a role in extracellular matrix stabilization through their binding to hyaluronic acid 7. Bikunin and ITI heavy chains have been proposed to be involved in carcinogenesis and metastasis, and they can contribute to inflammation as acute-phase proteins in various conditions. Few data are available on their differential expression during carcinogenesis, pointing to the loss of ITI heavy chains in human solid tumors 8. Current RNA-seq approaches have embarked on a systematic collection of gene expression data from various human tissues, which are particularly useful to characterize members of gene families and propose differential functions and activities in as yet disregarded tissues. Data made available in the Expression Atlas 9 illustrate the prospects of these experiments. An overview of RNA-seq results (Illumina Human Body Map; 10) regarding the ITI heavy chain genes ITIH1–ITIH5 (Fig. 1) demonstrates that ITIH1–ITIH4 are predominantly expressed in liver and ITIH5 though is mainly expressed in breast, adipose tissue and placenta. A recent study published in Experimental Dermatology 11 has now investigated the importance of ITIH5 (OMIM 609783) in skin, where it is moderately expressed, in contrast to the absent expression of ITIH1–ITIH4 (Fig. 1). Based on the finding of gene expression obtained with a targeted microarray-based approach in liver and skin, the authors have demonstrated that ITIH5 is found in normal dermal fibroblasts, but not in epidermal keratinocytes. Interestingly, they found an upregulation in inflammatory skin diseases, namely psoriasis, atopic dermatitis and allergic contact dermatitis. ITIH5 was identified in these conditions in suprabasal layers of the epidermis, in particular in the respective areas of immune reactions. The importance of ITIs for inflammatory disorders is further suggested by their accumulation in lichen sclerosus in the upper dermal areas where hyaluronan is abnormally deposited 12. The study of epidermal ITIs sheds light on the role of hyaluronan for epidermal structure and function. Itih5 knockout mice and ITIH5-deficient murine epidermal equivalents showed thinning of the epidermis, reduced proliferative capacities and disturbed epidermal cornification 11. On the other hand, application of exogenous hyaluronan to skin equivalents resulted in increased proliferation and enhanced development of the epidermal lipid barrier 13. Hyaluronan signalling is mediated through CD44 binding and supposed to be enhanced by ITI heavy chains and other hyaluronan-associated proteins 7. It is essential for proper keratinocyte differentiation, where it is potentially implemented by the elevation of intracellular Ca2+ levels 14. Regulatory pathways in the skin involving ITIH5 have not been explored so far, but they might give exciting new insight into basic cutaneous mechanisms including wound healing and skin ageing. The finding of ITIH5 in the skin underlines the importance of global gene expression studies for the understanding of tissue function and disease. Functional studies of signalling pathways and protein networks are now required, and advanced model systems, necessarily also models representing human tissues and human cells, are on the way for systematic analyses in a larger scale. Unrecognized regulatory molecules, however, can give decisive clues to mechanisms of epidermal homeostasis. The author has no conflict of interest to declare.

title: Sex differences in mechanisms of disease
abstract: Nearly every known mental illness and neurological disorder afflicts both men and women, but very few affect them at equal rates. These discrepancies in disease prevalence suggest that biological sex may contribute to a person's risk and etiology of a given disorder, and therefore, understanding the influence of sex on disease mechanisms is critical for preclinical research. The articles in this issue—the second of two G2B Special Issues on sex differences—work toward this exact goal. Covering research in rodents and humans and topics ranging from maternal care, stress, substance abuse and Alzheimer's models, we offer a diverse look at the many ways in which sex, genetics and experience interact to shape brain health. Common to the emergence of many mental illnesses is exposure to stress, and sex differences in how stress impacts the brain likely contribute to sex-dependent outcomes in disease risk, symptoms and recovery. Two reviews on this topic lead the issue. First, Shaw et al1 examine one of the most stress-sensitive developmental periods, adolescence. They focus on the prefrontal cortex, which continues to mature throughout adolescence, undergoing critical windows of structural plasticity in both gray and white matter. That these key periods of synaptic pruning and myelination coincide with puberty provides a perfect opportunity for stress to elicit long-term, sexually divergent effects on brain structure, function and health. The authors pull from both human and rodent literature to describe the current state of evidence for these sex-dependent outcomes, drawing connections to the development of mental illness and neurological disorders. In the second review, Brivio et al2 take a brain-wide look at sexual dimorphism in stress-induced gene expression in both clinical populations and animal studies. They discuss the complex factors that can contribute to observed alterations in gene transcription, including stress modality, timing and experimental techniques used. They also provide exceptionally useful tables that outline acute and chronic stress effects on the expression of dozens of genes, broken down by animal sex and strain, brain region and type of stressor—a fantastic resource for our readers. Women are particularly susceptible to mood and anxiety disorders, and several research papers in this issue identify potential mechanisms underlying this imbalance. Kreutzmann et al3 report that previous exposure to foot shock stress improves safety learning in male mice, but not females, an effect that was dependent on neuropeptide S. In a new mouse model of stress-induced binge eating,4 females exhibited increased binging after a “frustration stress” experience, while poststress eating in males stayed constant. Stress can also lead to reinstatement of drug-seeking behavior, an effect observed equally in male and female mice. However, Lee et al5 show that the ability of the drug guanfacine to prevent stress-induced reinstatement of nicotine-seeking behavior in a conditioned place preference test depends on a novel interaction between sex and individual animals' preferred test chamber at baseline, suggesting a role for sex-dependent context processing in the likelihood of substance abuse treatments being successful. Other aspects of addiction—such as substance type, age of initiation, and abuse trajectories—have clear sex and gender differences, suggesting a need for sex-specific evaluation of addiction mechanisms. In a thoughtful review of both clinical and preclinical evidence, Datta et al6 argue that parallel genomic studies in human and model organisms represent a promising investigative strategy toward this end. Finally, a review by Booher et al7 explores the current literature on exercise as an ameliorative agent in animal models of alcohol use disorder. Although the vast majority of this work has been carried out only in male mice and rats, the studies that were conducted on both sexes suggest that exercise may be even more beneficial to females than it is in males. Two papers in this issue examine factors that can disrupt a behavior that is (at least in most laboratory rodents) uniquely female—maternal care—which can have long-lasting effects on offspring development and mental health. Reshetnikov et al8 find that prolonged separation from their pups during the first 2 weeks of life causes a robust decrease in pup licking, an effect accompanied by cell loss in the hippocampus and spatial memory deficits. Poor maternal care was also observed in mice with a double knockout (dKO) of two diacylglycerol kinase genes (eta and iota).9 dKO dams were deficient at pup retrieval and did not appear to feed their pups as often, resulting in only a 30% pup survival rate after postnatal day 3. These rodent papers are complemented by a review of the human literature connecting maternal caregiving behavior to DNA methylation in offspring.10 Notably, the authors include a discussion of the impact that maternal depression can have on epigenetic outcomes in children, especially in stress- and inflammation-related genes. Finally, two articles investigate potential sex differences in the 5xFAD mouse model of Alzheimer's disease (AD). AD is both more prevalent and more severe in women, but as in many fields, relevant preclinical research has been conducted primarily in male animals. Characterization of behavioral phenotypes in female genetic models will, therefore, be a critical step in determining their utility for understanding sex-dependent AD symptoms and disease trajectories. An extensive battery of locomotor behavior across the adult lifespan (age 3-16 months) showed that, despite robust motor deficits in 5xFAD mice of both sexes and a few age-dependent sex differences, very few sex × genotype interactions could be observed.11 Along similar lines, Grant et al12 found that whisking behavior in several exploratory tasks depended more on sex and the presence of retinal degeneration than on the 5xFAD genotype itself. Taken together, these studies suggest that this particular mutant may not be ideal for studying the aspects of AD that are sex-dependent. Collectively, the articles here show a clear need to consider sex a biological variable when investigating the molecular mechanisms that underlie disease symptomatology and treatments. We look forward to increased submissions to G2B in which data represent both male and female subjects, thus shedding a more balanced light on potential therapeutic targets for mental and neurological disorders.

title: dock11 Knockdown in Zebrafish Disrupts Embryogenesis: Insights Into the Genetic Causes of Early Pregnancy Loss
abstract: Recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL), affecting approximately 5% of couples worldwide, represents a major challenge in reproductive medicine and causes psychological distress [1]. While embryonic chromosomal errors account for 40%–65% of early pregnancy losses, a substantial proportion of cases remain unexplained despite extensive clinical evaluation [2]. This diagnostic gap is further highlighted by the observation that pregnancy losses still occur even after the transfer of euploid embryos following preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A) in assisted reproduction [3]. This clinical dilemma underscores a critical gap in our understanding of the molecular pathogenesis of early pregnancy loss, particularly the role of embryonic-intrinsic factors [2-4]. While existing research has largely centered on deficits in implantation and placental development, the critical window of early embryogenesis—a period governed by the embryo's autonomous developmental program and fundamental to embryonic survival—has received comparatively less attention [5-7]. Our previous multi-omics analysis of chorionic villi from euploid pregnancy-loss patients revealed epigenetic silencing of DOCK11 (dedicator of cytokinesis 11) and its consequent transcriptional downregulation in extra-embryonic tissues, implicating DOCK11 as a potential contributor to pregnancy failure (our unpublished data). This finding prompted us to investigate the potential intrinsic role of DOCK11 within the embryo proper. To functionally validate the role of DOCK11 in early embryogenesis, we turned to the zebrafish model. This model is uniquely suited for such an investigation, as its external development and optical transparency enable direct visualization of embryogenesis while being free from the confounding influences of the maternal uterine environment and placental function. Morpholino (MO)-mediated knockdown of dock11 was confirmed via a significant reduction in its mRNA levels (Figure 1A). Dock11-knockdown embryos exhibited markedly compromised viability, with significantly reduced hatching rates and elevated embryonic mortality compared to wild-type (WT) controls (Figure 1B,C). Detailed morphological assessment revealed a spectrum of severe developmental defects, including pronounced axial curvature, a high incidence of malformations, and reduced overall body length (Figure 1D). To determine the impact on early patterning, we further performed whole-mount in situ hybridization. Although the spatial domains of key lineage markers—including gsc and chd (dorsal mesoderm, assessed at 5 hpf), bmp4 and eve1 (ventral mesoderm, 5 hpf), ntl (axial mesoderm, assessed 8 hpf), sox17 (endoderm, 8 hpf), and gata2a (ectoderm, 8 hpf) —remained largely unaltered in dock11 MO embryos compared to WT embryos, their expression levels were markedly altered: the expression of chd was significantly increased, while that of gsc, eve1, sox17, and gata2a was decreased. Changes in bmp4 and ntl were not significant (Figure 1E). Collectively, these findings establish that dock11 is essential for normal embryogenesis and germ layer formation in zebrafish. Having established that the loss of dock11 disrupts early embryonic development in zebrafish, we next sought to delineate the underlying molecular mechanisms. We first characterised the spatiotemporal expression profile of dock11, finding its mRNA to be dynamically expressed, with a pronounced peak at 5 h post-fertilisation (hpf, Figure 2A)—a stage immediately preceding the onset of gastrulation that is critical for establishing the molecular patterns underlying subsequent cell fate determination. We therefore conducted transcriptomic profiling at this critical stage. RNA-seq analysis revealed extensive dysregulation in dock11 morphants, with 796 upregulated and 243 downregulated (Figure 2B,C, Table S1). Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis of these differentially expressed genes revealed enrichment in pathways related to embryonic development, including VEGF signalling, tight junction assembly, Hippo and MAPK signalling pathways (Figure 2D, Table S2). Furthermore, pathways governing cell fate, such as apoptosis, p53 signalling, ferroptosis, and cellular senescence, were prominently enriched, as were metabolic regulators like PPAR and AMPK signalling, and mRNA surveillance mechanisms (Figure 2D, Table S2). Gene ontology (GO) analysis of cellular component highlighted structures essential for tissue integrity and morphogenesis, including the extracellular matrix (ECM), endoplasmic reticulum membrane, ion-channel complexes, the basolateral plasma membrane, and cell–cell junctions. Enrichment was also observed for cytoskeletal elements and vesicle-related complexes (Figure 2E, Table S3). These results strongly suggest that dock11 regulates a broad transcriptional network essential for cell adhesion, intra-cellular signalling, and the maintenance of lineage integrity during early embryogenesis. It is noteworthy that while previous studies using dock11 knockout models in mice and zebrafish reported no embryonic lethality but rather focused on immune and hematopoietic phenotypes [8, 9], our study focuses on the role of dock11 during early embryogenesis. In conclusion, our integrated findings suggest the importance of embryonic-intrinsic factors in pregnancy loss. We demonstrate that dock11 is essential for body patterning and germ layer specification in the early vertebrate embryo. This work thus expands our understanding of the genetic aetiology of early pregnancy loss and establishes DOCK11 dysfunction as a previously unappreciated mechanistic contributor to the aetiology of early pregnancy loss. title: Epigenetics: Reprogrammable interface of the genome and environments
abstract: In the past decade, the genes involved in the pathogenesis of type 1 and type 2 diabetes have been identified by a comprehensive search over the whole genome, the genome‐wide association study (GWAS). The method is now carried out by a dramatically improved technique to detect single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with different frequency between the control and the disease group. SNP, however, is not an universal disease‐marker that can be used in any case. For different ethnicities in particular, it is necessary to clarify the difference of the contribution of the gene. Therefore, data of Asian populations would be as significant, and this Journal is considered to further increase the importance in this field. In clinical applications of gene‐based medicine, it is also necessary to carry out a longitudinal study of these candidate genes. Even with the genome‐wide study, we cannot apply the information to an individual patient. Genetic taylor‐made medicine will become possible only when evidence is obtained by carrying out a longitudinal prospective study on the gene of interest. Recently, a new additional area called ‘epigenetics’ has emerged in the field of complex genetic diseases, including diabetes mellitus. Epigenesis refers to a process that is based on the information marked on the genome after fertilization, primarily in animals. This has been elucidated as a mechanism of cellular function, specifically the pattern of gene expression through change of chromatin structure instead of change in the nucleotide sequences. Biochemical entities of the epigenetic marks include deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) modifications, such as 5‐methylcytosine at CpG sites, and post‐translational modifications of histones methylation, acetylation and phosphorylation. These are subject to being erased throughout the entire genome in germ line cells, but it comes to appear again after fertilization, and will change according to the specific cellular environment and differentiation. With the exception of this process, epigenetic status can be determined according to parental origin of the allele for genomic imprinting, and can be determined randomly for X chromosome inactivation. Importantly, epigenetic system ensures two outstanding property at the same time. First, the systems shows robust epigenetic memory that is crucial for maintenance of cellular differentiation states even through the process of somatic cell division. Second, the system applies the flexibility of chromatin states to adaptation and responses to various environmental challenges from outside the cell. So, what gene region should we observe to find alterations in an epigenome for etiology and new regenerative medicine? A simple method is to analyze known candidate genes. Most of the associated genes of type 2 diabetes found by GWAS appear to have the potential to regulate β‐cell mass and function. In fact, studies on candidate genes including peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor gamma gene, the insulin gene promoter and the pancreatic and duodenal homeobox 1 gene promoter identified epigenetic alterations in pancreatic islets of patients with type 2 diabetes. Alternatively, comprehensive studies that address the role of epigenetic alterations in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes in humans have recently commenced to uncover genes with differential DNA methylation in diabetic islets compared with controls1. The approach for screening the open chromatin with gene activity or non‐coding ribonucleic acid (RNA) has been used for genome‐wide epigenetic analysis. These techniques have allowed researchers to map epigenetic marks with gene activity2, or the transcribed long non‐coding RNAs3. The results show a new class of islet genes providing a new impact on the pathophysiology of diabetes. As observed in many Asian countries, the prevalence of type 2 diabetes in the population where the incidence of type 2 diabetes was once low is now increasing greatly in accordance with the change of nutritional status. The genes responsible for metabolic control might alter their expression patterns through alterations of epigenetic status and adapt to the nutritional change, but the precise mechanism of this epigenetic reprogramming is not fully clarified. Strong epidemiological and experimental evidence shows a link between intrauterine growth restriction and adult diseases, such as type 2 diabetes4. This is thought to be an example of the changes in epigenetic programming as a result of nutritional status. Another important concept of epigenetic phenomena in diabetes is the age‐associated alteration of epigenetic status, specifically of genes in pancreatic β‐cells. Islet β‐cells can expand during embryonic development and the neonatal period in humans and experimental animals, but the ability of proliferation subsequently decreases. The disability of β‐cells to divide for renewal in later life is thought to be based on cellular senescence, which mainly contributes to the aging phenotype in general. Three molecular mechanisms of cellular senescence that have attracted attention include: (i) upregulation of the cyclin‐dependent kinase inhibitor, p16INK4a; (ii) accumulation of oxidative DNA damage; and (iii) telomere shortening (Figure 1). Figure 1 Schematic presentation of epigenetic and environmental process of β‐cell senescence. Three major factors of cellular senescence (INK4a‐ARF, deoxyribonucleic acid [DNA] damage and telomere loss) are known as Hayflick factors. Of ... Prior studies suggest that the Polycomb group (PcG) protein enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (Ezh2) functions as a histone methyl‐transferase (H3K27 trimethylation; H3K27me3), and is an epigenetic regulator of critical genes, embryonic development, stem cell renewal and cellular senescence. Most importantly, Ezh2 represses the INK4a/ARF locus as a target gene region in islet β‐cells through epigenetic alterations in a time‐dependent manner. Thus, the epigenetic investigation of the failure in β‐cell regeneration through the INK4a/ARF locus and PcG protein might elucidate underlying diabetes pathogenesis. Finally, epigenetic studies can provide novel regenerative medicine. Now researchers are beginning to think that they could investigate the ability of β‐cell self‐renewal independently of its differentiation status by attributing an epigenetic status that is reprogrammable. Furthermore, a recent study suggested that the epigenetic memory might predispose even β‐cell derived‐induced pluripotent stem cells to differentiate more readily into insulin‐producing cells5. If epigenomic manipulation becomes possible, the reprogramming of patients' cells should provide novel regeneration therapies for diabetes.

title: Vitamin D: One hundred years on
abstract: The year 2022 will feature in history books for a number of reasons; but in the world of nutrition, it marks the Centenary of the landmark investigation by Dame Harriette Chick and her co-workers. Exactly 100 years ago, working with malnourished children in a clinic in Vienna shortly after the First World War, they showed that rickets in children in Austria could be prevented or cured by cod liver oil supplementation. This cod liver oil was subsequently recognised as a particularly rich source of vitamin D (Chick et al., 1922). A century later, vitamin D continues to be a specific hot topic as evidenced by the number of papers published in recent years in Nutrition Bulletin (Allen et al., 2014; Buttriss & Lanham-New, 2020; Clark et al., 2021; Gibson-Moore, 2021; Guo et al., 2019; Hengist et al., 2019; Lanham-New et al., 2022; Mendes et al., 2018; Smith & Hart, 2017; Spiro & Buttriss, 2014; Tripkovic, 2013; Tripkovic et al., 2017; Wilson-Barnes et al., 2020). These papers have been brought together in a specially curated Virtual Issue [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/toc/10.1111/(ISSN)1467-3010.Vitamin-D-Centenary]. Dame Harriette Chick was awarded the British Nutrition Foundation (BNF) Prize in 1974 for her contribution to nutrition research. By then already a Centenarian, she chose her ground-breaking research on vitamin D as the theme for her BNF Annual Lecture (Chick, 1976), in which she summarised her work in Vienna, Austria in 1919–1922, presenting the chemical, clinical and sociological aspects of her story. Dame Harriette worked at the Lister Institute of Preventative Medicine, London, United Kingdom from 1905 to 1970, and she and colleagues were sent to Vienna by the Accessory Food Factor Committee of the Medical Research Council to investigate whether the diseases affecting the population were the result of vitamin deficiencies (Figure 1). Over the past century, many researchers—far too many to mention here—have contributed to our current understanding of vitamin D and its role as a pro-hormone. Dame Harriette's findings in the 1920s built on research over the previous couple of decades in the United States and Europe. This included exploration of the hypothesis (Hopkins, 1920) that essential dietary factors are necessary to prevent diseases such as scurvy and rickets (both of which had been described hundreds of years previously); and the work led by a British doctor, Mellanby (Mellanby, 1919), who had become concerned about the very high incidence of rickets in the United Kingdom, especially in Scotland. Following a series of trials, Mellanby realised that puppies fed on a diet based on the oatmeal-rich Scottish diet (and coincidentally housed indoors), developed rickets which could be prevented or cured by the addition of cod liver oil (see Wolf (2004) for more details). Mellanby concluded that it ‘seems probable that the cause of rickets is a diminished intake of an antirachitic factor which is either fat-soluble factor A’, previously identified by McCollum and Davis (1914) and later known as vitamin A ‘or has a similar distribution’ (Figure 2). Again in 1922, a key experiment by McCollum et al. (1922) showed that heated, oxidised cod liver oil could cure rickets in rats but could not prevent xerophthalmia (now known to be a symptom of vitamin A deficiency). The antirachitic factor was given the name vitamin D (as B and C had already been used for water-soluble factors and the anti-scurvy factor, respectively). Meanwhile, an entirely different cure for rickets had emerged, namely ultraviolet (UV) light. It had long been acknowledged that fresh air and sunshine were effective in the prevention of rickets, as discussed by Dr Egon Kodicek from Cambridge (United Kingdom) who was awarded the BNF Prize in 1973 for his work on vitamin D (Kodicek, 1974a). In 1921, Hess and Unger suggested that the seasonal incidence of rickets was due to seasonal variations in sunlight exposure (Hess & Unger, 1921). At about the same time, Huldschinsky and colleagues in Berlin (Germany) had observed that UV radiation from a mercury vapour lamp had a healing effect in rickets (see Chick, 1976). Support for this was evident in the work of Chick et al. (1922) in Vienna, who observed that sunlight would cure rickets in young children just as well as cod liver oil. A group of 12 infants received therapeutic exposure to sunlight and this was found to be effective in restoring normal bone. Furthermore, those receiving the combination of sunlight exposure and cod liver oil healed most rapidly. Using X-ray analysis, Dame Harriette and her co-workers showed conclusively that rickets had a marked winter incidence; that protection in winter could be achieved by diet (none of the infants given cod liver oil developed rickets) and that infants in the first 6 months of life were particularly susceptible to rickets. During the 1920s, three teams of scientists in London, Göttingen (Germany) and New York (United States) worked collaboratively to identify chemically the substance in skin now known to be the UV-activated precursor of vitamin D, 7-dehydrocholesterol. In 1928, Adolf Windaus at the University of Göttingen received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on this (see Wolf (2004) for more details). In his 1973 BNF Prize Lecture, Kodicek described how understanding of the role of UV light, in converting a precursor of vitamin D in the skin into an active form of the vitamin, followed on a few years after the work in Vienna, and he summarised work by himself and others, over the following 50 years, that built on these important discoveries a century ago (Kodicek, 1974a, 1974b). In 1969, a specific binding protein for vitamin D, the vitamin D receptor, was identified and the metabolism of vitamin D in the liver and kidney to its active forms was elucidated. It was Fraser and Kodicek (1970) who demonstrated the conversion in the kidney of the liver-hydroxylated vitamin D metabolite, 25-hydroxy vitamin D3 (25-OH-D3), to what was later identified, by Holick, DeLuca and colleagues (Holick et al., 1971), as calcitriol (1,25-[OH]2D3) (Figure 3). In a relatively recent historical overview, Professor Hector DeLuca from Wisconsin University (United States) (DeLuca, 2008) summarises key discoveries such as the conversion of vitamin D to its hormonal form, its regulation and the evolving picture of its molecular mechanism of action. He discusses how it has long been recognised that calcitriol circulates as a hormone in the blood, regulating the concentrations of calcium and phosphate in the bloodstream and promoting growth and remodelling of bone. Furthermore, over time, evidence continues to emerge to show that vitamin D's role extends far beyond mineralisation of the skeleton to, for example, muscle function, the immune system and treating the skin disorder psoriasis (see Lanham-New et al., 2022). As discussed later, vitamin D's role in the immune system (Hewison, 2012, 2022) was explored in considerable depth in relation to the coronavirus pandemic (Lanham-New et al., 2020) and this has been summarised in Nutrition Bulletin by Gibson-Moore (2021). These developments, which began more than a century ago, underpin the science that supports policies to tackle the incidence of rickets that continue to this day. Between the two World Wars, the incidence of rickets declined as a result of use of cod liver oil as a supplement for children and also the increased exposure to sunshine as a result of slum clearances and the reduction in industrial and domestic smoke. In the 1930s onwards, public health initiatives recommending cod liver oil for young children and fortification of foods such as margarine or milk with vitamin D, resulted in rickets being largely eradicated in westernised countries in the post-war years. But thereafter, particularly in recent decades, incidence has been on the increase, particularly in some ethnic minority groups. Hospitalisation rates for rickets were low in the 1960s and 1970s and declined further in the 1980s and 1990s but increased in the 2000s. For a historical perspective of childhood rickets, see Goldacre et al. (2014). There are relatively few dietary sources of vitamin D (see Buttriss & Lanham-New, 2020). Apart from cod liver oil, the richest are oil-rich fish and egg yolks. Other sources include meat/meat products and fortified foods, such as some fat spreads, some breakfast cereals, some dairy products (especially yogurts) and vitamin D fortified dairy alternatives. Further information can be found in Allen et al. (2014). In 1940, the vitamin D fortification of margarine became mandatory in the UK (see DH, 1991), but this requirement ceased in 2013 as products defined as margarine had largely been superseded by reduced fat spreads which were outside the scope of the Regulation (Defra, 2014). In the United States, liquid milk is fortified routinely on a voluntary basis, but this is not the situation in the United Kingdom. Other foods fortified on a voluntary basis include breakfast cereals (about 75%), milk substitutes (slightly more than 50%), yogurts (about 25%) and cheeses, juices and spreads (OHID, 2022). In Canada, milk and margarine fortification with vitamin D is a legal requirement and fortified plant-based drinks must contain an amount equivalent to that in cows' milk. Infant formula is also fortified on a mandatory basis in Canada and many other countries including the United Kingdom. Opportunities for enrichment of foods with vitamin D are discussed in papers included in the Virtual Issue (Buttriss & Lanham-New, 2020; Kiely & Cashman, 2018; Lanham-New et al., 2022) and include enrichment of eggs by manipulating the hens' diet (Clark et al., 2021). Until 2016, there were no UK dietary vitamin D recommendations for the general population—just for groups considered to be ‘at risk’ of vitamin D deficiency (infants and young children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, people over 65 years, those who are housebound and people with darker skin pigmentation) (DH, 1991). The Committee on Medical Aspects of Food and Nutrition Policy (COMA) had concluded that since vitamin D is synthesised in the skin when it is exposed to sunlight, dietary intakes of vitamin D were not necessary for most of the UK population (aged 4–64 years) (DH, 1991). It was assumed that skin synthesis of vitamin D in the summer would be enough to cover requirements during the winter. The situation changed in 2016 when the UK's Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition (SACN) set Reference Nutrient Intakes (RNI), for all children over the age of 1 year and all adults (including pregnant and breastfeeding women), of 10 μg/day (400 IU/day) of vitamin D to achieve a 25(OH)D serum concentration of above 25 nmol/L (SACN, 2016). Safe intakes of 8.5–10 μg/day (340–400 IU/day) were established for younger children up to 1 year of age (more detail below). SACN did not take account of sunlight exposure in making recommendations because of the number and complexity of factors that affect skin synthesis of vitamin D (see Buttriss et al., 2022). The RNI and safe intakes were developed to ensure that the majority of the UK population would have enough vitamin D to protect musculoskeletal health, all year round. It should be noted that a lack of vitamin D dose–response trials in children and adolescents has hindered the development of evidence-based dietary requirements for vitamin D in these population subgroups. In this context, Smith and Hart (2017) discuss the findings of two recent randomised controlled trials, conducted as part of the EU-funded vitamin D project ODIN led by University College Cork (Kiely et al., 2015). At the time of SACN's report, UK vitamin D intakes from diet were typically considerably lower than the new RNI (see Buttriss et al., 2022) and, in response to SACN's (2016) recommendations, the UK Government changed its advice on vitamin D intake. It recommended that everyone considers taking a vitamin D supplement (10 μg/day) in the winter months (between October and March), and that some at-risk groups including people who are not often outdoors such as frail, elderly or housebound people, and those with dark skin, consider taking a vitamin D (10 μg) supplement throughout the year. The vulnerability of young children to developing rickets was recognised a century ago in Dame Harriette Chick's work, and in policy put in place since that time. Yet, cases of rickets continue and low vitamin D status is widespread in the community (Uday & Högler, 2018). UK Government advice is that babies from birth to 1 year should have a daily supplement containing 8.5–10 μg throughout the year if they are breastfed or if they are formula-fed but consume less than 500 ml/day (because infant formulae are already fortified with vitamin D by law). Children aged 1–4 years should also have a daily supplement throughout the year (10 μg) (Public Health England, 2016). A number of papers on vitamin D have featured in Nutrition Bulletin over recent years and these are now specifically curated in a Virtual Issue of the journal. A paper by Spiro and Buttriss (2014) illustrated that although public health policy varies to some extent when European countries are compared, there is evidence of low vitamin D status in sections of the population in countries across Europe regardless of latitude. Furthermore, as discussed by Mendes et al. (2018) in the context of Brazil, despite abundant sunshine, vitamin D insufficiency appears more prevalent than expected in countries far closer to the Equator. Vitamin D has been associated with a wide range of health outcomes, but controversies remain as to the exact nature and extent of the majority of these relationships; and whether associations are in the causal pathway. These controversies are discussed in a report from a recent workshop funded by the Medical Research Council (Lanham-New et al., 2022). The objectives of the Workshop were twofold: to elucidate the role of vitamin D in human health; and to develop strategies to improve vitamin D status in the UK population. Not surprisingly, one of the topics discussed was COVID-19, because one of the emerging areas of interest is immune health (Lanham-New et al., 2020). A rapid review by SACN in 2020 in relation to vitamin D and risk of acute respiratory tract infections (ARTI), suggested that overall there may be some benefit from daily, low-dose vitamin D in reducing risk, even though the size of any potential benefit may be small (SACN, 2020). The work of Professor Adrian Martineau (Queen Mary University, London) has been pivotal in the vitamin D/ARTI field (Jolliffe et al., 2020, 2021; Martineau et al., 2017). In the COVID-19 pandemic, minority ethnic groups have been shown to be at increased risk of more severe outcomes compared with their white European counterparts which has been associated with low vitamin D status, although causation has yet to be determined (SACN, 2020). A paper by Gibson-Moore (2021) provides a summary of recent work on this topic. Using data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey (NDNS) and the UK Biobank cohort, stark ethnic differences in vitamin D status have emerged, with dark-skinned population groups at more risk of low vitamin D status (serum levels <25/30 nmol/L) compared to white European groups (see Lanham-New et al., 2022). Furthermore, studies have also shown that South Asian population subgroups living in the UK have much less seasonal variation in vitamin D status (i.e. the increase and decrease in serum 25(OH)D levels with transition from UVB-rich summer to UVB-poor winter, respectively) than is evident in white population subgroups. This higher risk of year round low vitamin D status has implications for bone health but also possibly for some non-skeletal health outcomes (see Lanham-New et al., 2022). Recent data suggest that dark-skinned populations may need at least twice the currently recommended daily intake of vitamin D in order to reach an adequate serum 25(OH)D concentration throughout the year (Cashman et al., 2022), an area in which further research is urgently warranted. Review of safe upper limits for vitamin D is currently underway under the auspices of the European Food Safety Authority. Another population group prone to low vitamin D status is people living with obesity. Despite evidence that vitamin D accumulates substantially in adipose tissue, individuals with obesity often have serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations below 25 nmol/L, indicative of risk of deficiency. Thus, it appears that vitamin D can become ‘trapped’ in adipose tissue, potentially due to insufficient lipolytic stimulation and/or due to tissue dysfunction/adaptation resulting from adipose expansion. Hengist et al. (2019) discuss emerging evidence suggesting that exercise may mobilise vitamin D from adipose tissue (even in the absence of weight loss). In another Nutrition Bulletin paper, Wilson-Barnes et al. (2020) explore the effects of vitamin D on physical performance for recreational and professional athletes and also military recruits, in particular muscular strength, stress fractures, cardiovascular health and incidence of illness including upper respiratory tract infections. Despite the change in advice regarding vitamin D supplementation in the United Kingdom in 2016, the latest NDNS data (years 2016–2019) for the UK shows that 19%, 16% and 13% of children aged 11–18 years, adults aged 19–64 years and adults aged 65 years and over, respectively, had serum 25(OH)D concentrations below 25 nmol/L (Bates et al., 2020). This indicates that increased risk of vitamin D deficiency remains, and that Government advice is not being adhered to. title: Maternal obesity: influencing the heart right from the start
abstract: Children of women with obesity have a higher risk of cardiovascular and metabolic disease. Understanding how maternal obesity affects the heart of offspring during development might provide an evidence base for lifestyle and other interventions during pregnancy or in early childhood to reduce future cardiovascular risk. Several clinical and experimental studies have investigated how obesity during pregnancy predisposes offspring to hypertension, insulin resistance, obesity, cardiovascular disease and premature mortality (Shrestha et al., 2021). However, few studies have considered whether the sex of the offspring influences cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes. In this issue of The Journal of Physiology, Vaughan and colleagues use their established mouse model of maternal obesity to investigate the metabolic disturbances underpinning adverse cardiac remodelling and dysfunction in offspring of obese dams (Vaughan et al., 2022). A strength of the study is that the authors assessed cardiac function of both male and female offspring up to 2 years of age (the approximate lifespan of a mouse). This longitudinal assessment extends their previous findings, which revealed the emergence of diastolic dysfunction by 3 months of age in male offspring of obese dams and at 6 months of age in female mice (Vaughan et al., 2020). Although group sizes at some time points might have been too small to reveal subtle changes in function, the present study points to a persistent impairment in diastolic function in male offspring of obese dams throughout lifespan, and a progressive worsening of diastolic function in females. The authors speculate that this sexual dimorphism might be attributable to the cardioprotective effects of oestrogen, because the marked decline in diastolic dysfunction observed in female mice at 9 months of age coincides approximately with a decline in circulating oestradiol in the mouse strain used. Additional studies are needed to draw further conclusions regarding the cardioprotective effects of oestrogen and the role of androgens and progestogens in this setting. Both male and female fetuses of obese dams were heavier and had significantly heavier hearts (even when normalized to body weight) than fetuses from control dams. Interestingly, cardiac hypertrophy was no longer evident in offspring of obese dams at 6 months of age, and body weight had also normalized. Histopathological changes (e.g. interstitial fibrosis and capillary density) were not examined at either time point. To investigate transcriptional changes associated with fetal cardiac hypertrophy, the authors conducted RNA sequencing and downstream pathway analyses on fetal heart samples 18.5 days postcoitum. The overall transcriptomic response to maternal obesity was strongly influenced by sex, with only 66 commonly altered genes between males and females. Ingenuity analysis identified contrasting macromolecular pathways upregulated by maternal obesity: lipid synthesis and metabolism in males, and carbohydrate uptake in females. These data suggest that metabolic perturbances in response to maternal obesity are influenced by sex, despite exposure to the same metabolic milieu in utero. A key finding of this study was the identification of Pparg, the gene encoding peroxisome proliferator activated receptor gamma (PPARγ), as a critical node of the fetal myocardial transcriptomic response to maternal overnutrition. PPARγ is a ligand-activated transcription factor responsible for modulating the expression of genes involved in fatty acid uptake, oxidation and storage in the heart. The PPARγ agonist pioglitazone is used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes and reduces the risk of major adverse cardiovascular outcomes in diabetic patients (Liao et al., 2017; Sinha & Ghosal, 2020). However, pioglitazone also increases the risk of heart failure (Liao et al., 2017; Sinha & Ghosal, 2020), and transgenic overexpression of Pparg in mice leads to cardiac hypertrophy and systolic dysfunction (Son et al., 2007), indicating a potential structural and functional role for this key metabolic protein. In this study, Vaughan et al. (2022) report that Pparg expression was increased in both male and female hearts at embryonic day 18.5 and at 6 months of age and was strongly correlated with diastolic dysfunction (E/E′ ratio) in male animals and with left ventricular end-diastolic volume in female animals. Follow-up experiments in adult offspring revealed differential expression of Pparg target genes (e.g. Acox1) in male and female hearts despite a comparable increase in Pparg expression, suggesting sexual dimorphism in the post-transcriptional regulation of PPARγ function, for example by co-regulators or other interacting proteins. A recent investigation identified PPARα as a key modulator of the fetal cardiac lipidome in response to maternal obesity (Pantaleao et al., 2022), and dual activation of PPARα and PPARγ induces cardiac dysfunction in mice (Kalliora et al., 2019). Thus, further investigation into this important family of metabolic regulators will be important for improving our understanding of the cardiometabolic response to overnutrition in utero. Finally, the authors measured cardiac lipid and glucose uptake, in addition to respiration in left ventricular tissue, to examine energy metabolism between male and female adult offspring. Perturbations in fatty acid oxidation were observed in male offspring of obese dams, and females had impaired myocardial glucose uptake. Lipid uptake was not altered by maternal obesity in either sex. Interestingly, impaired glucose uptake in the female mice was not accompanied by differences in expression of the major cardiac glucose transporters, GLUT1 or GLUT4, although Western blot analysis revealed a reduction in insulin receptor phosphorylation suggestive of insulin resistance. Collectively, these data suggest that metabolic programming in utero sets the stage for myocardial metabolism throughout life, with an increased reliance on fatty acids (via different mechanisms) in adult male and female offspring. In summary, this paper adds to the growing body of evidence that maternal obesity reprograms cardiac metabolism of offspring, with lasting effects on cardiac function. Importantly, it reveals differences in cardiac metabolic and functional responses of male and female offspring to maternal obesity. Improved understanding of the mechanisms underpinning these responses will take us a step closer to developing sex-specific strategies to mitigate the detrimental cardiometabolic consequences of an obesogenic in utero environment. title: Epigenome–proteome integration in aged skeletal muscle after exercise training
abstract: Epigenomic alterations in skeletal muscle after acute exercise and chronic training are becoming more established. In particular, modifications to the DNA methylome (e.g., but not limited to; Pilotto et al., 2024; Seaborne et al., 2018) and how they affect corresponding alterations in transcript expression (Turner et al., 2019 reviewed in Sharples (2024)). However, in skeletal muscle it is not yet well established how alterations in the DNA methylome after training feed through to alterations at the protein level. Exciting and recent multi-omic meta-analysis studies in humans have begun to investigate whether any relationships exist between the methylome and proteome after exercise training (Jacques et al., 2023, 2024). However, across the field in humans there are currently fewer proteome samples to compare with the methylome (especially relative to many transcriptome samples). Furthermore, when using paired samples, although shifts in DNA methylation occur in relevant exercise pathways following training (reviewed by Egan & Sharples, 2023; Sharples & Turner, 2023), methylome analyses that includes hundreds of thousands or even millions of DNA sites (with many sites within each gene) may become a challenge when directly comparing statistical approaches in proteomic data sets. The Molecular Transducers of Physical Activity Consortium (MoTrPAC) have recently begun to explore the multi-omic adaptations after endurance exercise training in genetically identical rats (reviewed in Sharples, 2024); however, the integration of the paired methylome–proteome has not yet been conducted in aged muscle following an exercise training intervention. Kevin Murach and Yuan Wen's teams attempt to bridge an important gap in epigenome–proteome association in skeletal muscle after exercise training in aged mice (22–24 months old) (Chambers et al., 2025). Importantly, late-life exercise has previously been associated with epigenetic reprogramming in mouse skeletal muscle (Murach et al., 2022). Higher levels of aerobic exercise in older age (Voisin et al., 2023), after disease (Gorski et al., 2023) and following resistance training (Blocquiaux et al., 2022; Ruple et al., 2021) have also been associated with restoration of the epigenetic landscape in human skeletal muscle. Using their established mouse model of 8 weeks progressive weighted wheel running (PoWeR) the authors implemented exercise training in aged mice (22–24 months old) and integrated the methylome and proteome of the resulting gastrocnemius muscle compared with a control group of age-matched sedentary control animals (Chambers et al., 2025). The prominent effect of PoWeR training was evident at the methylome (with 4,999 differentially methylated CpG sites identified, ∼13% of measured CpGs) and the proteome level (1,032 proteins significantly altered, with 90% of these upregulated). DNA methylome responses after PoWeR training identified alterations that have been described in human skeletal muscle after exercise, such as differential methylation of the nuclear receptor 4A (NR4A) genes (Maasar et al., 2021) and homeobox (HOX) genes that have been demonstrated to be influenced by age and physical activity levels (Turner et al., 2020). The group were also able to integrate the methylome and proteome data using an algorithm called binding and expression target analysis (BETA). For use in methylome data, BETA takes the locations of the differential methylated CpGs and combines the magnitude of change, significance and their location/distance relative to gene regulatory regions to provide a ‘regulatory potential score’. Therefore, this tool identifies genes and proteins that are more likely to be regulated by the epigenetic changes that are detected. Subsequently, pathway enrichment can also be performed on the genes that are predicted by BETA. This is a useful tool within the field, because there are often many single CpGs altered amongst thousands of genes (and many CpGs within the same gene) identified in skeletal muscle following acute exercise and after chronic training. Typically, to account for this, differential methylated region (DMR) analysis is performed to identify genes with multiple CpGs altered in the same direction in small regions of the same gene. BETA extends this approach with the magnitude of change and distance to known regulatory regions. Therefore, for discovery or hypothesis-generating purposes, BETA analysis could also help to further support DMR analysis and provide crucial information on the genes likely to be altered at the expression or protein level with a higher degree of confidence. Then, by using paired transcriptomic or proteomic analysis of the same samples, it is then possible directly to associate the hypothesis-generating BETA prediction of the epigenetic regulation of the gene with the quantitative confirmation of the alteration at the gene and/or protein level. Previously, using BETA, the group had identified epigenetic regulation of mitochondrial function genes in mouse skeletal muscle after mechanical overload-induced hypertrophy that matched muscle respirometry analysis (Ismaeel et al., 2024), suggesting an important epigenetic component in the regulation of metabolic pathways after muscle adaptation. In the present study, following PoWeR training, BETA predicted the epigenetic regulation of 216 upregulated proteins. Pathway enrichment of these proteins identified epigenetic regulation of protein translation, with the majority of genes belonging to ribosomal (RPL6, RPL18, RPL29, RPL31, RPLP0, RPS10 and RPS14) and mitochondrial ribosomal processes (MRPL1, MRPL2, MRPL4, MRPL10, MRPL11, MRPL14, MRPL28, MRPL37, MRPL43, MRPL45, MRPL46, MRPL53, MRPS11, MRPS22 and MRPS25) in addition to the eukaryotic initiation factors (EIFs) involved in the initiation of protein translation in the ribosome (EIF2B3, EIF2B4, EIF2B5 and EIF3D). Furthermore, together with the above alterations, NADH proteins and those in the electron transport chain (ETC) complex 1 were epigenetically regulated genes that were also upregulated at the protein level (NDUFA2, NDUFA3, NDUFA8, NDUFB3, NDUFB9, NDUFB11, NDUFC2, NDUFS1, NDUFS2, NDUFS6, NDUFS7 and NDUFV3). Overall, highlighting metabolic processes associated with energy metabolism, mitochondrial protein synthesis and protein translation seem to be the most prominent epigenetically regulated processess following exercise training in aged muscle. BETA also predicted epigenetic regulation of LACTB, MIB1 and UBR4, with MIB1 and UBR4 both being E3-ubiquitin ligases. Indeed, UBR4 and UBR5 have been identified as important in muscle mass regulation in model organisms and humans (Hughes et al., 2021; Hunt et al., 2019; Seaborne et al., 2019). Computationally the authors also undertook Landscape In Silico deletion Analysis (LISA) using the BETA upregulated proteins as an input. LISA uses ChiP-sequencing data and computation to predict transcriptional regulators likely to be involved in the gene (or ultimately the protein) response. Using LISA, Proto-Oncogene C-Myc (MYC) was highlighted as a transcription factor using both the genes corresponding to upregulated proteins predicted by BETA and the global proteome response. MYC overexpression in skeletal muscle can alter DNA methylation (Jones et al., 2023); therefore, this study adds to accumulating evidence that MYC is likely to be an important regulator of the epigenetic landscape that might subsequently impact the protein-level response to exercise training in ageing skeletal muscle. With respect to the exercise training protocol in mice, a limitation of the study is that PoWeR is not a perfect analogue for exercise training, e.g. resistance or aerobic. PoWeR does, however, include combined higher loading parameters together with a continuous contraction regime of both progressive resistance and continuous wheel running, leading to adaptation characteristic of both resistance and endurance training (reviewed by Murach et al., 2020). Where PoWeR also presents a more relevant physiological exercise stimulus without being invasive in comparison to other mouse models such as synergist ablation. Therefore, the PoWeR model, alongside other recent models, such as implanted electrical stimulation (Spillover) (Schmoll et al., 2018), serves as an important rodent model to investigate molecular responses and adaptation to exercise, perhaps lending itself to combined loading/intensity exercise stimuli that would perhaps be more reflective of the majority of mixed sports that combine both a resistance and a continuous element (Egan & Sharples, 2023). For methylome analyses, the authors use a custom Horvath mammalian array of ∼36K CpG site coverage on the DNA. Although this is much smaller coverage than Illumina EPIC arrays (now version 2 EPICs arrays cover ∼1 million CpGs) and much lower in comparison to bisulphite sequencing technology, the Horvath arrays are designed to cover conserved CpGs across mammalian species and are important in predicting epigenetic ageing. Therefore, making interpretation and translation across species more likely, in addition for it being possible to study known epigenetic biomarkers of ageing. Consequently, it is also interesting that, in the present study, the 36K assay identifies some age-related CpGs after exercise training in old mice, and again suggests that the epigenetic landscape altered by age itself could be influenced positively by exercise training (Blocquiaux et al., 2022; Gorski et al., 2023; Murach et al., 2022; Ruple et al., 2021; Turner et al., 2020; Voisin et al., 2023). In the future, although the largest proportion of nuclei in human skeletal muscle tissue are myonuclei, hence whole-tissue DNA analysis is perhaps reflective of changes across the tissue niche, it seems that there might be a distinct epigenomic contribution of the other cell types resident within skeletal muscle tissue (Wen et al., 2021). Therefore, it would be an interesting avenue for the field to explore the methylome at the single nuclei or single muscle fibre resolution and also to investigate other epigenetic modifications, such as chromatin accessibly (via ATAC-seq), that might precede or interact with DNA methylation changes to alter transcriptional and translational potential after exercise training (reviewed in: Sharples, 2024).
